lesson.title: Turning Observation Into Data: Measurement in Chemistry
lesson.summary: This section covers how chemists quantify observations, distinguishing accuracy from precision and working through a significant figures calculation.
lesson.body:
The scientific method depends on evidence, and in chemistry that evidence almost always takes the form of measurements: quantitative observations that pair a number with a unit, like twenty five milliliters or ninety eight point six degrees Fahrenheit, rather than vague qualitative descriptions like a lot or warm. When the earlier section described testing whether humidity affects corrosion, actually running that experiment requires measuring humidity levels, exposure times, and the mass of corrosion product, all with real instruments and real numbers. Without measurement, a hypothesis can never be genuinely tested, since there would be no consistent way to compare the outcome of one trial to another or to describe results precisely enough for another scientist to check.

Every measurement carries some degree of uncertainty, because no instrument is perfectly precise, and chemists use two related but distinct words to describe the quality of a set of measurements: accuracy and precision. Accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the true, correct value. Precision describes how close repeated measurements are to each other, regardless of whether they are close to the true value. A balance that reads 15.98 g, 16.01 g, and 15.99 g for the same object every time is precise, because the readings cluster tightly, and if the object's actual mass is 16.00 g, those readings are also accurate. A different balance that consistently reads 14.50 g, 14.51 g, and 14.49 g for that same object is still precise, but not accurate, since it is consistently off from the true value, likely due to a calibration error. A measurement can be precise without being accurate, and in principle accurate on average without being precise, if scattered readings happen to average out close to the true value.

Because every measuring instrument has a limited precision, chemists record measurements using significant figures, a system for showing exactly how precisely a quantity is known. A significant figure is any digit in a measurement that is known with confidence, plus one final estimated digit. A graduated cylinder marked in 1 milliliter increments might let you read a volume as 24.6 mL, with the 24 read directly off the marked lines and the final 6 estimated between them; writing that measurement as 24.60 mL would falsely claim more precision than the instrument actually provides. Significant figures matter just as much in calculations as in direct readings. As a worked example, if a solid's mass is measured as 12.42 g, four significant figures, and its volume is measured as 4.10 cm3, three significant figures, using a less precise instrument, its density is 12.42 divided by 4.10, which equals 3.0293 on a calculator, but the answer must be rounded to three significant figures, since a calculated result cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement used to find it, giving a final answer of 3.03 g/cm3.

Careful measurement is what turns a hypothesis from an untested guess into a claim supported by real evidence, and it is also what allows one scientist's results to be meaningfully compared against another's, whether they are working in the same lab or on opposite sides of the world. That comparison only works, however, if everyone is measuring in the same units, using the same defined standards for a gram, a meter, and a second. That shared system of standardized units, essential to making any measurement meaningful beyond the lab it was taken in, is exactly the subject of the next section.
